legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Critique of Agent Model", Eric Xing, Mingkai Deng, Jinyu Hou (MBZUAI / CMU); arXiv 2606.23991v1 [cs.AI], dated 15 June 2026 (arXiv stamp 22 Jun 2026); preprint.

COVERAGE: all 147,541 chars read (44 pages: body, references, Appendices A-D). Nothing skipped. References only skimmed for origins.

EMPIRICAL STATUS: This is a POSITION/THEORY paper. It has no experiments, no tables, no benchmark numbers and no baselines. Its only "results" are four theorems with proof sketches, which hold under stated assumptions. Empirical evidence is deferred to companion manuscripts that I did NOT read: [23] Deng et al. 2026 "General agentic planning through simulative reasoning with world models" and [24] Deng et al., arXiv 2605.22138. The paper says: "Our preliminary results [23, 24] provide initial evidence along the Performance and Efficiency dimensions; Growth evaluation remains an important direction for future work." (p.29). Do not cite any performance number from this paper.

CLAIMS (ranked; no numeric empirical results exist, so number = "none" unless a formula)
1. Definition of agent model, kept distinct from the world model. An agent is a policy p_pi(a|s,g,i) (state, goal, identity), and the agent/universe split follows from the trajectory factorization.
 number: none (Eq. 1; Eq. 7-8 for GIC)
 setup: formal definition; a world model is the learned universe factor p_mu(s'|s,a), the agent model the agent factor.
 quote: "an agent model (AM) is a reasoning model that generates real-world actions based on its goals g and identity i. Formally, an AM π maps the current world state s to a predicted action a through, for example, a conditional probability distribution: pπ(a | s, g, i)."
 where: p.3 (lines 88-99); the factorization is on p.4.
2. Central distinction: agentic (competence in external scaffolding) vs agentive (competence internalized). Current LLM agents are called agentic, not agentive.
 number: none
 setup: conceptual; five axes are goal, identity, decision-making, self-regulation, learning. Coordination is a sixth axis (§2.7).
 quote: "Current AI systems are largely agentic but not yet agentive: much of their competence resides in their workflows and harnesses, not in the model itself. Consequently, such systems are often better understood as sophisticated software pipelines rather than genuinely autonomous agents."
 where: p.2.
3. Landscape taxonomy of things labelled "agent": program-based bots (thermostat, ELIZA, Selenium); LLM wrapper systems (DeerFlow, AutoGen, Cursor); LLM-centered systems trained end-to-end (Claude Code, Operator, DeepSeek-V4); model-less physical systems (industrial robots); embodied-model systems (VLAs, world action models).
 quote: "The organization of behavior thus resides in the engineering around the model, not in the model's own decision-making." (wrapper systems). For LLM-centered systems: "goals still depend on human-specified short-term instructions; identity remains externally defined; decision-making relies on unregulated chain-of-thought; and behavioral change still requires retraining or prompt redesign".
 where: pp.8-10.
4. Definitions of the dimensions as a spectrum from externally prescribed to internally maintained.
 - Goals: externally given gt versus persistent g decomposed by module delta.
 - Identity: static i0 (system prompt, config) versus evolving i_t.
 - Decision-making: fixed workflow or MPC versus simulative reasoning (System II) plus actor (System I).
 - Self-regulation: a configurator kappa picks the mode (System III).
 - Learning: external training loop versus self-governed.
 - Multi-agent: "better understood as a single scaffolded system consisting of a federation of tasks rather than a genuine multi-agent society."
 where: pp.5-8.
5. Critique of the harness-engineering practice (relevant to model + loop + tools + memory).
 quote: "current practice exogenizes what should be part of genuine agency: the formation and evolution of one's own identity."
 Identity is "implemented as a hand-written system prompt describing the agent's role, available tools, and behavioral constraints." They explicitly name MCP, Agent Skills and harness engineering (citing OpenAI [49], Anthropic [65]) as the practice criticized. They also say "designing strong interfaces for the agent is clearly valuable".
 where: p.12.
6. Chain-of-thought is not planning. Reasoning tokens give "narrative plausibility", not grounded dynamics.
 quote: "prediction based on narrative plausibility (e.g., token probability) rather than real-world consistency, with no guarantee of correct planning."
 Also: "Without such grounding, more reasoning tokens can simply mean more opportunities for confident but unfounded extrapolation."
 setup: argument, no experiment; cites [32] Gema et al. (inverse scaling in test-time compute) and [73] Su et al. for "longer reasoning does not necessarily yield better answers".
 where: p.15 and p.17.
7. Theorem 2 (world-model planning never hurts). Given a world model with total-variation error <= eps, any baseline policy can be augmented to a mixed policy with V(pi_mix) >= V(pi).
 number: eps_model = 2*gamma*Rmax*eps/(1-gamma)^2 (the margin).
 setup: tabular-style MDP; bounded reward; discount gamma in (0,1); the mixed policy adopts the plan only if the predicted advantage exceeds 2*eps_model. Proof uses the Simulation Lemma and the Performance Difference Lemma. Guarantee is "vacuous" if the world model is trained on reward.
 quote: "if a reasonably accurate world model exists, any baseline policy can be augmented with it to obtain a mixed policy π_mix that is at least as good, if not better."
 where: p.16, Appendix B.
8. Theorem 3 (always-on MPC horizon grows with precision). H = O((1/(1-gamma))(log(1/eps) + 2 log(1/(1-gamma)) + log Cmax)), so H = O(log(1/eps)) for constant gamma and Cmax. Suboptimality bound 2*gamma^H*Cmax/(1-gamma)^2.
 setup: cost perfectly aligned with reward; planning inside the world model f only.
 where: p.17, Appendix C. This is a standard value-iteration bound used rhetorically against always-on MPC. Note that log(1/eps) growth is mild, so the "unsustainable" label in Fig. 6 is rhetoric, not a result.
9. Theorem 1 (fast-slow beats slow-only). Revising an identity or self-model per step gives regret <= Regret_std - Omega(sum Nk).
 setup: relies on assumptions A1 (identity revisions are better than random, with delta1, delta2 < 1/2) and A2 (the slow update is monotone). The proof gives E[Delta] >= (1-delta)*lambda - delta*B > 0 when lambda/B > delta/(1-delta).
 quote: "if fast updates in practice produce identity revisions that are better than random, the fast-slow agent learning accumulates strictly less regret in expectation than slow-only learning".
 where: p.13, Appendix A. The result is conditional on the assumption it largely restates.
10. Theorem 4 (mixing simulated and real experience). V(pi_mix*) >= V(pi_env*) - 2*C*alpha*eps, where C = 2*gamma*Rmax/(1-gamma)^2. It dominates when the world model is perfect.
 setup: fixed real data budget; mixture environment M_alpha. The proof is trivial because the policy class contains the real-only class.
 where: p.20-21, Appendix D.
11. Proposal GIC (Goal-Identity-Configurator): belief encoder h, goal decomposer delta, identity evolver iota, configurator kappa (System III), simulative planner (System II), actor alpha (System I), a critic, and a separately trained world model. Factorization in Eq. 7-8. Three-phase training: pretraining, simulative RL, real deployment. Evaluation proposed as PEG (Performance, Efficiency, Growth). Not implemented here.
 where: pp.23-31.
12. Safety claim. The paper claims modular GIC means harm reduces to goal misspecification or component error.
 quote: "for a sufficiently well-trained system, harmful behavior converges to zero unless the goal itself is wrong."
 where: p.30. Unsupported assertion; flag as such.
 Also on multi-agent: "Natural agents exhibit a further capacity for self-organization" (§2.7).

LIMITS:
- No experiments, ablations or baselines in this paper. All empirical support is deferred to unread companions [23, 24] (the authors' own).
- The definition of "agentive" is the authors' own and contested. It is a spectrum, and no operational test is given. "Difficulty" for evaluating the configurator is conceded as "an open problem in its own right."
- The theorems are standard RL bounds (Simulation Lemma, Performance Difference Lemma). They need an accurate world model with a known TV bound, which is not shown to be attainable in open domains.
- The Theorem 1 assumption A1 essentially assumes the conclusion.
- The authors have a stake: they promote their own world-model line (PAN, GLP, [85] "Critiques of world models") and criticize LeCun's JEPA/MPC and joint world-action models. Expect the bias.
- Authors concede: "Our intent is not to offer definitive answers" (§6). The Growth evaluation is future work.
- The paper dates fast (2026 product names such as Opus 4.7, GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V4; blog and X-post citations).
- It gives no standard textbook definition of an LLM agent (model + loop + tools + memory). It treats that as the "agentic" scaffolding it critiques. For the note it is a counter-definition, not a source for the loop itself.
- Memory appears only as "associative memory" caching plans (p.16, Fig. 7) and as a survey mention (Wang et al. [76]: profiling, memory, planning, action).

BUILDS ON: Xing, Deng, Hou, Hu 2025 "Critiques of world models" [85] (arXiv 2507.05169); LeCun 2022 "A path towards autonomous machine intelligence" [45] (configurator, MPC, System-style modules); Kahneman 2011 [38] (System I/II); Sutton and Barto 1998 [74] (value function); Kearns and Singh 2002 [43] (Simulation Lemma); Kakade and Langford 2002 [39] (Performance Difference Lemma); Kakade 2001 [40]; Schulman et al. 2015 [67] (TRPO); Wei et al. 2022 [79] (CoT); Guo et al. 2025 [33] (R1); Shinn et al. 2023 [70] (Reflexion, criticized as text-only reflection); Wang et al. 2024 [76] and other agent surveys [27, 31, 37, 80, 17] (criticized for taking "agency" for granted); Descartes 1641, Aristotle, Kant 1781; Bostrom 2014, Amodei et al. 2016 and Russell 2019 (safety); Xiang et al. 2025 PAN [84]; Mitchell et al. 2018 "Never-ending learning" [53].

CODE: none. Equations worth keeping (verbatim, p.4):
 "pπµ(at, st+1, ..., sT | st) = prod_k pπ(ak | sk) pµ(sk+1 | sk, ak)"  (agent factor times universe factor)
 Eq. 7 factorization p_GIC(a_t|o_t,g,i_{t-1}) = sum p_alpha(a|s,c) p_pi_f(c|s,g,i,u) p_kappa(u|s,g,i) p_iota(i|s,i_prev) p_delta(g_t|s,g) p_h(s|o)  (p.26).

FIGURES (pymupdf captions run):
- Fig. 2 (p.4): "Illustration of an agent acting in an environment to achieve a goal." Policy, world state, goal, critic and universe. A minimal agent-environment loop diagram; the best figure candidate for the note's loop definition.
- Fig. 8 (p.24): GIC architecture, with the pilot use case. Shows the six components and Systems I-III on one page.
- Fig. 3 (p.12): step-by-step subgoals versus hierarchical decomposition.
- Fig. 5 (p.15): reactive policy versus simulative reasoning.
- Fig. 7 (p.19): MPC versus configurator.
- Fig. 1 (p.3), Fig. 4 (p.14) and Fig. 6 (p.18) are conceptual sketches with no data.
Fig. 2 is the one worth reusing; Figs. 4 and 6 are schematic curves, not measurements.

PROBLEMS: The extraction is clean text but math is garbled (subscripts, fractions). No scanned pages. No embedded instructions found in the PDF text. The "Theorem 1 Omega(sum Nk)" statement is the abstract form; the appendix gives the explicit decomposition. The Eq. 3 and Eq. 7 layouts are partly scrambled, so I did not quote them verbatim beyond the above. Companion papers [23, 24] were not available and were not read.
